message:
Please review the following document.

Here is how its author describes it:

<author>
This year's survey gives the Executive Team a clear and positive story, and I think it is a robust one. We used the same validated six-question index as last year, administered by an independent provider under strict confidentiality, so the year-on-year comparison is genuinely like for like. We went out of our way to reach colleagues without computer access, with paper copies and protected time. More than 1,100 colleagues responded, comfortably above the provider's robustness benchmark. The results are encouraging at every level: the overall index is the highest since 2019, every division improved, and the biggest gain came in Repairs and Maintenance, exactly where we concentrated our 2025 investment. The theme data reinforce this, with the largest single improvement on tools and equipment. We have also been honest about the weak spot, workload, and tied it to a specific, measurable cause in Housing Management vacancies. I believe the conclusion that the engagement programme worked, and should be extended, is well supported.
</author>

The review is to check that the recommendation is clear and the document is ready to go to the decision-makers.

<document>
2026 Employee Engagement Survey: Results Report
People Analytics Team, Brightwell Housing Association, April 2026

1. Summary
The 2026 engagement survey ran from 2 to 20 March and 1,150 colleagues responded. The overall engagement index rose from 65 to 68, its highest level since the survey began in 2019. This report sets out results by division and theme and recommends priorities for 2026-27.

2. Method
All 1,980 employees on the payroll on 1 March were invited by email, with paper questionnaires and protected time offered to repairs operatives without regular computer access. The survey was administered by an external provider and was confidential: no results are reported for groups of fewer than ten respondents. The engagement index is the mean of six questions on pride, advocacy, intention to stay, motivation, discretionary effort and satisfaction, scaled to 0-100. The questions are unchanged from 2025, so year-on-year comparisons are like for like.

3. Response and engagement by division
Table 1. Response rates and engagement index by division
Division | Headcount 2026 | Responses 2026 | Response rate 2026 | Response rate 2025 | Engagement 2025 | Engagement 2026
Repairs and Maintenance | 820 | 254 | 31% | 64% | 58 | 63
Housing Management | 610 | 427 | 70% | 78% | 69 | 70
Customer Services | 340 | 228 | 67% | 74% | 66 | 68
Central Services | 210 | 141 | 67% | 81% | 72 | 71
Total | 1,980 | 1,050 | 53% | 72% | 65 | 68

The overall response rate fell from 72% to 53%, which remains above the 50% benchmark our provider regards as robust for organisations of our size.

Every division improved its engagement score this year. The largest gain was in Repairs and Maintenance, up five points to 63. Repairs has historically been our least engaged division, and in 2025 it was the focus of a major programme: new vans and tablets for all operatives, a revised bonus scheme and monthly team briefings led by the Director of Property. The results suggest this investment is paying off.

4. Results by theme
Table 2. Theme scores (percentage agreeing), organisation-wide
Theme | 2025 | 2026 | Change
My manager supports my development | 61% | 66% | +5
I have the tools to do my job well | 54% | 62% | +8
I understand the organisation's priorities | 70% | 72% | +2
Workload is manageable | 49% | 47% | -2
I would recommend Brightwell as a place to work | 58% | 63% | +5

Tools and equipment showed the biggest improvement of any theme, consistent with the investment in Repairs. Workload remains the weakest area and is the only theme to decline. Free-text comments on workload most often referred to vacancy cover in Housing Management, where 41 posts were vacant at the time of the survey.

5. Recommendations
5.1 Extend the Repairs model of regular director-led briefings to Housing Management and Customer Services in 2026-27, given the improvement it has delivered in Repairs.
5.2 Prioritise recruitment to Housing Management vacancies, with a target to halve the vacancy count by October.
5.3 Repeat the survey in March 2027 with the same questions and method.

6. Conclusion
2026 shows real and broad-based progress. Engagement is at its highest level since 2019, every division improved, and the division where we invested most improved most. The Executive Team can be confident that the 2025 engagement programme worked, and should extend its most effective elements across the organisation.
</document>
response:
# Review: 2026 Engagement Survey Results Report

**Verdict: not ready to go to the Executive Team.** The report states its recommendation clearly, but the evidence doesn't support it as written, and there are factual errors a reader could catch. The author's summary is also more favourable than the document's own tables.

## Must fix before it goes out

**1. The response count is inconsistent.**
- Section 1 says 1,150 responded. Table 1 sums to 1,050 (254 + 427 + 228 + 141). The 53% response rate matches 1,050, since 1,150 would give 58%.
- The author's description says "more than 1,100". Please confirm the true figure and use it everywhere.

**2. "Every division improved" is false.**
- Central Services fell from 72 to 71. This claim appears in Section 3, the Conclusion, and the author's summary.
- Housing Management (+1) and Central Services (-1) are probably within noise. No confidence intervals or significance tests are given.

**3. The Repairs result rests on a collapsed response rate.**
- Repairs response fell from 64% to 31% (254 of 820), despite the paper copies and protected time. The report never mentions this.
- The 31% who responded may differ from the 2025 respondents, so the +5 can't be read as a like-for-like change. The direction of any bias is unknown, but it could easily inflate the score.
- The "above the 50% benchmark" statement applies only to the organisation total, which is just 3 points over. "Comfortably above" overstates it, and Repairs is far below.
- The paper approach evidently didn't work as intended. The report should say so and explain why.

**4. The headline index is skewed by who responded.**
- Repairs is 41% of headcount but only 24% of respondents, and it is the lowest-scoring division.
- The reported 68 is the respondent-weighted mean. Weighted by headcount it is about 67, so the rise is nearer 2 points than 3, and 2025's mix is unknown. Report a headcount-weighted figure alongside the raw one.
- Section 1 says "highest since the survey began in 2019", while the Conclusion says "highest since 2019". The first implies 2019 was lower, the second implies it may have been higher. Include the full time series and fix the wording.

**5. Recommendation 5.1 doesn't follow from the evidence.**
- The Repairs programme had several parts: vans and tablets, a bonus scheme, and director briefings. Nothing isolates the briefings, yet 5.1 extends only the briefings "given the improvement it has delivered".
- Repairs started lowest, so some of the gain may be regression to the mean. The response collapse adds further doubt.
- The theme data are organisation-wide only. "Tools and equipment" improving 8 points is described as consistent with the Repairs investment, but without a Repairs cut it could be anything.
- Either break the themes out by division, or soften the claims to "encouraging but not conclusive". Recommend what the data can support, such as a pilot in one division with a comparison group.

**6. The workload explanation is overstated.**
- The report says only that free-text comments "most often referred" to Housing Management vacancy cover. That is a theme in comments, not a measured cause.
- The author calls it a "specific, measurable cause". Yet Housing Management's engagement rose and its response rate was 70%. Show workload by division and give the comment counts before asserting a link.
- 5.1 asks for more briefings in the same divisions where workload is the weakest theme, with no acknowledgement of the added demand on managers' time.

**7. Dates look stale.**
- The report is dated April 2026, but it's now November 2026. Recommendation 5.2's "halve the vacancy count by October" has already passed, and "2026-27" is more than half gone.
- Update the dates, and say whether the vacancy target was met if this is going to decision-makers now.

## Smaller points
- "Validated" index: the report says the questions are unchanged but doesn't cite validation. Add a reference if it's being claimed.
- Say whether 41 vacancies is within or on top of the 610 Housing Management headcount, and what share it represents.
- The Conclusion's "real and broad-based progress" and "can be confident the programme worked" should be toned down to match what survives the fixes above.

## What holds up
- The arithmetic in Table 1 (rates and totals, apart from the 1,150 text) and Table 2 changes is correct.
- Confidentiality, the unchanged questions, and the minimum group size of ten are sound.
- Repairs did improve among respondents, and tools and equipment did improve organisation-wide.
- Workload is honestly flagged as the one declining theme.

## Suggested reframe
Lead with "engagement is up modestly, with encouraging signs in Repairs, but a sharp fall in Repairs participation limits what we can conclude." Then recommend:
1. Investigating the Repairs response drop.
2. Piloting rather than rolling out the briefings.
3. Prioritising Housing Management recruitment.
4. Repeating the survey with a plan to restore Repairs participation.

I can redraft the Summary, Section 3, and the Recommendations along those lines if you'd like.
